summary: Specifies Wave and Equation Based Rate Control (WEBRC), a congestion control building block for IP multicast. Receivers join the same session at different rates depending on their connections, and no feedback to the sender is needed because it is receiver-driven. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: One sender shares data with many listeners. Each listener picks how fast to receive based on their own connection, so no one slows the others.

subtitle: Receiver-driven congestion control for IP multicast, where each listener picks its own rate by joining wave channels.

tldr.problem: A single multicast sender serving very many receivers over different network paths cannot use sender-side feedback, yet it still needs congestion control that is fair to TCP.
tldr.mechanism: The sender spreads packets over a base channel and many wave channels whose rates decay over time. Each receiver measures its loss and multicast round-trip time, computes a TCP-like target rate, and joins or leaves wave channels to match it.
tldr.outcome: Receivers adjust independently and need no feedback to the sender, so a slow receiver does not slow faster ones. The scheme was published as Experimental, with the working group intending to resubmit it as a Proposed Standard once it was deemed adequate.

today: RFC 3738 is an Experimental RFC from April 2004, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. Its Statement of Intent says the RMT working group planned to resubmit the specification as a Proposed Standard once the scheme was deemed adequate.

sections.title: What WEBRC Is and Where It Fits
sections.content:
Wave and Equation Based Rate Control (WEBRC) is a congestion control building block designed to be massively scalable with IP multicast. It is receiver-driven: all measurements and decisions to raise or lower the rate are made by each receiver and acted on by sending join and leave messages to the network. It adjusts the reception rate without regard to reliability, unlike TCP, where the two are interwoven. It is designed to compete reasonably fairly with TCP, meaning generally within a factor of two of a TCP flow's rate, with much smoother throughput, at the price of responding more slowly to changes.

WEBRC provides congestion control only. It does not identify which session or object a packet belongs to, and it provides no reliability. It is meant to be combined with other building blocks, for example LCT can carry its header information and FEC codes can add reliability. It is most applicable to objects or streams of substantial length, from hundreds of kilobytes to many gigabytes, transferred over tens of seconds or more.

Receivers use IGMP for IPv4 multicast and MLDv2 for IPv6 to join and leave channels, the only dependency on IP version. WEBRC works with both Any-Source Multicast and Source-Specific Multicast, but SSM makes channel allocation easier and has security advantages. It assumes the route from sender to a receiver is the same for all channels in a session, so with ASM the sender is RECOMMENDED to register all channels with the same RP, placed as close as possible to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: WEBRC is only the speed-control part of sending to a crowd. It does not decide what is sent or fix lost pieces, other parts do that.

sections.title: Base Channel and Wave Channels
sections.content:
A session is a set of channels from one sender, each identified by a (sender address, multicast group) pair. There is one base channel and T wave channels. Time is split into slots of TSD seconds, and a current time slot index (CTSI) counts up modulo T so receivers can loosely synchronize.

On the base channel the packet rate starts at BCR_P at the beginning of a slot and falls to P*BCR_P by its end. Each wave channel is active for N slots: its rate jumps to a high value, then drops by a factor of P per slot until it reaches BCR_P, followed by a quiescent period in which nothing is sent, then the cycle repeats. Waves are spaced TSD seconds apart.

Active wave channels are ordered into layers; the lowest is the one nearest the end of its wave. A receiver always joins the base channel first, then joins consecutive layers from the lowest upward, and MUST leave a wave channel when it goes quiescent. The earlier in a wave a receiver joins, the higher its rate. To go lower it simply stops joining new waves, because existing waves decay on their own.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a row of taps that each start fully open and slowly close. Joining a tap early gets you a big flow; joining late gets a trickle. You choose when to hop on each one.

sections.title: Sender Parameters
sections.content:
The sender's main input is SR_b, an upper bound on the aggregate sending rate in bits per second; it is RECOMMENDED to keep the aggregate rate constant. Secondary inputs mostly keep default values:

  • LENP_B: packet length in bytes, SHOULD be as high as possible without causing fragmentation.
  • BCR_P: base channel starting rate in packets per second, default 1.
  • TSD: time slot duration, RECOMMENDED 10 seconds.
  • QD: minimum quiescent period, RECOMMENDED 300 seconds.
  • P: multiplicative drop in each channel rate per slot, default 0.75.
  • N: duration of each wave in slots, also the number of active wave channels.

From these the sender derives Q, the number of quiescent slots (the ceiling of QD/TSD), and T = N + Q, the total number of wave channels. The base channel has channel number T and the wave channels have 0 to T-1. Packets carry sequence numbers (PSN) that count per channel, and the last packet of a wave carries the maximum PSN so receivers can tell a wave has ended. Except for at most the first two slots of a wave, the rate MUST fall exponentially by P per slot, which leaves room to shape the start of a wave so the total sending rate is constant.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender picks how long each wave lasts, how fast it fades, and how long to rest before starting again. The sender never has to know how many listeners there are.

sections.title: How a Receiver Decides to Join
sections.content:
Most of WEBRC's complexity is in the receiver, which follows TFRC. It keeps a target rate and joins the next layer only if the rate after joining would be at most the target. Two estimates drive the target: LOSSP, the average loss probability, and ARTT, the average multicast round-trip time (MRTT).

LOSSP uses two exponentially weighted filters, a time-based one and a loss-based one, with recommended smoothing constants of 0.3 each. The MRTT is measured from the time a join is sent to the arrival of the first packet from that channel, and smoothed with a recommended constant of 0.25. The rate equation REQN is the TCP-like equation taken from TFRC. Decisions are made once per epoch, recommended as 0.5 seconds (TSD/20).

A slow start mode ramps up quickly at the start of a session and after a sharp rate drop; it ends on a packet loss, a sharp MRTT increase, reaching the maximum rate, or arrival rate not following the last join. A receiver MUST NOT join the next layer when the first base packet has not arrived, a loss event or a join is in progress, or it already has all N layers, and MUST NOT join if the target rate is too low. A loss event covers all losses in the following ARTT seconds. A receiver MUST leave the session if no packets arrive for a long period (RECOMMENDED threshold max{10,TSD} seconds) or the time slot index does not change for a long period (RECOMMENDED max{20,2*TSD} seconds).
sections.plainLanguage: Each listener watches how many pieces get lost and how long replies take, works out a safe speed like a careful driver, and only takes the next tap when the speed is safe.

sections.title: Congestion Control Information Fields
sections.content:
Every packet MUST carry Congestion Control Information with three fields: the CTSI, the channel number (CN) and the packet sequence number (PSN). The RFC defines a short format of 32 bits and a long format of 64 bits, and recommends using one of them, although protocols may define their own compatible format. Integers use network byte order.

In the short format CTSI and CN are 8 bits each and the PSN is 16 bits, so T MUST be at most 255. In the long format CTSI and CN are 16 bits and the PSN is 32 bits, so T MUST be at most 65,535. The PSN is scoped by channel, and the last packet of a wave carries the maximum value (2^16-1 or 2^32-1 respectively).
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a small label saying which time slot it is, which tap it came from, and its number in line, so listeners can spot missing pieces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
WEBRC can be attacked by injecting forged packets into the multicast stream to confuse receivers. The damage falls mostly on elements and receivers downstream of the attack. The RFC RECOMMENDS Reverse Path Forwarding checks on all routers and switches between sender and receivers.

It also RECOMMENDS authenticating each packet on receipt, but notes there are no practical multicast schemes giving instant authentication. TESLA can authenticate packets a few seconds later, for example to end a session after detecting a forged packet, but the normal WEBRC responses should still happen immediately. Receivers with faulty implementations can harm the network and other receivers, so receivers should identify themselves as legitimate before getting the session description, and measures should prevent acceptance of an incorrect session description.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could slip in fake packets to confuse listeners. The RFC suggests checking where packets come from and making sure the listeners got the right instructions.

fields.name: CTSI
fields.desc: Current Time Slot Index, increases by one modulo T each TSD seconds.

fields.name: Channel Number
fields.desc: T for the base channel, 0 through T-1 for wave channels.

fields.name: Packet Sequence Number
fields.desc: Scoped by channel; the last packet of a wave carries 2^16-1.
